sentences: 25-LDC-0014 Planning Commission Staff Report July 25, 2026 Text Amendment to the Land Development Code – Data Center Location:

Text Amendment to the Land Development Code (LDC) related to Data Centers • Staff finds the text amendment is in keeping with Plan 2040 and recommends that the Planning Commission RECOMMEND that the Louisville Metro Council and other legislative bodies with zoning authority APPROVE the text amendment presented in this report CASE SUMMARY The Louisville Metro Council passed a resolution on September 25, 2025 requesting that staff and the Planning Commission review the Land Development Code (LDC) and develop recommendations to improve the regulations for data centers.
Data centers are buildings that house computer hardware that stores and processes digital information.
Currently, data centers are not classified as a specific use in the LDC.
Data centers that are in accessory in nature can be permitted in any zoning district in accordance with the accessory use standards.

In addition, “computer data centers” are listed as an acceptable activity for the underground space use, which is permitted with a conditional use permit in M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, PRO, C-M, C-2, and EZ-1.

Prohibit future data centers exceeding 500,000 sq ft, while allowing smaller-scale facilities that support existing employers and business needs within the community to more appropriate areas based on their size;
Restrict data centers that are over 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the M-3 district with a conditional use permit; 3.
Restrict data centers between 50,000 and 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the EZ-1, M-2, M- 3, and PEC districts and subject to special standards; and 4.

Only permit data centers that are less than 50,000 sq ft to manufacturing/ industrial areas in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC and PRO districts and subject to special standards (with an exception for telecommunication data centers in the C-3 district).

TECHNICAL REVIEW As data centers are currently permitted by right and do not require any local license or registration, the number of existing data centers is not tracked by any Louisville Metro Government agency.
Datacentermap.com, an online resource that provides locations and information related to data centers, indicated that were 23 data centers in Louisville as of July 23, 2026.

records.item: AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE LOUISVILLE METRO LAND DEVELOPMENT CODE REGARDING DATA CENTERS (CASE NO. 25-LDC-0014). O-251-26
sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.

Sincerely, Ashley Wilmes Executive Director and Attorney Kentucky Resources Council Tom FitzGerald Of Counsel Kentucky Resources Council Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org KRC Recommended Revisions to Louisville Metro Revised Draft Data Center Text Amendments This document presents the recommendations of Kentucky Resources Council concerning the revised Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC- 0014, July 20, 2026, Draft).

Introduction These recommendations are intended to ensure public notice and input, as well as a comprehensive and meaningful framework for regulating the location, operation, and decommissioning of all data centers.

The recommendations continue to suggest inclusion of many of the provisions in the Kentucky Resources Council (KRC) Model Data Center Zoning Ordinance, with respect to strengthening the review process, the quality of information submitted in applications, and the standards of performance for data center construction and operation.

Few of the recommendations on the initial draft were incorporated into the current draft, and it is hoped that with further reflection, more of these concerns will be addressed in order to assure that data center siting, location, operation, and decommissioning will be done, if at all, in order to fully mitigate impacts and to respect other land uses and values.

Recommendations The July 20, 2026 revisions to the proposed Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, (and in some areas weaken the protections in the original draft), so that the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
Eliminate tiered approach to data center regulation.

The LMG text amendment takes a size-tiered approach, prohibiting data centers exceeding 500,000 square feet, requiring a conditional use permit for facilities between 250,001 and 500,000 square feet and treating smaller facilities as permitted uses with special standards in various industrial districts, subject only to registration with the Office of Planning and review by the Planning Director or designee, with no public notice or hearing opportunity.
With few exceptions, the LMG text amendment proposes the same standards and requirements for all tiers of data centers.
Yet for data center proposals below 250,000 square feet, the review process is abridged and public notice and comment eliminated in almost all instances.

KRC believes that the same standards and review process, including robust public involvement, should apply to all data centers that are subject to regulation, since those standards are self-differentiating and self-adjusting depending on the size, nature and intensity of the use. 2.

Text Amendment to the Land Development Code (LDC) related to Data Centers • Staff finds the text amendment is in keeping with Plan 2040 and recommends that the Planning Commission RECOMMEND that the Louisville Metro Council and other legislative bodies with zoning authority APPROVE the text amendment presented in this report CASE SUMMARY The Louisville Metro Council passed a resolution on September 25, 2025 requesting that staff and the Planning Commission review the Land Development Code (LDC) and develop recommendations to improve the regulations for data centers.
Data centers are buildings that house computer hardware that stores and processes digital information.
Currently, data centers are not classified as a specific use in the LDC.
Data centers that are in accessory in nature can be permitted in any zoning district in accordance with the accessory use standards.

In addition, “computer data centers” are listed as an acceptable activity for the underground space use, which is permitted with a conditional use permit in M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, PRO, C-M, C-2, and EZ-1.

Prohibit future data centers exceeding 500,000 sq ft, while allowing smaller-scale facilities that support existing employers and business needs within the community to more appropriate areas based on their size;
Restrict data centers that are over 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the M-3 district with a conditional use permit; 3.
Restrict data centers between 50,000 and 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the EZ-1, M-2, M- 3, and PEC districts and subject to special standards; and 4.

Only permit data centers that are less than 50,000 sq ft to manufacturing/ industrial areas in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC and PRO districts and subject to special standards (with an exception for telecommunication data centers in the C-3 district).

TECHNICAL REVIEW As data centers are currently permitted by right and do not require any local license or registration, the number of existing data centers is not tracked by any Louisville Metro Government agency.
Datacentermap.com, an online resource that provides locations and information related to data centers, indicated that were 23 data centers in Louisville as of July 23, 2026.

OPO —— Council Dee 126 www.kyrc.org ol KRC Summary of Revisions to Louisville Data Center Ordinance This document reviews the changes in the provisions of the proposed Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC-0014, June 9, 2026, Draft, revised following comment period on July 20, 2026.

The text of the revised proposed regulations, public comment form, and schedule for the public hearing dates for the Planning Commission to hear public comment are at: lidips://iouisvillekv.wouv/euveruuenl /olive-piduiiuy/Gala-cenlers Summary The revisions proposed to the draft Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, and the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
The review process remains at Director level or below for data centers of up to 250,000 sq. ft. in size unless a waiver is needed.

Revised proposal instead weakens the initial LMG proposal by eliminating conditional use permit requirement for telecommunications data centers except for those 50,001 to 250,000 that can't meet special standards.

The applicant is not required to submit plans as part of the application, demonstrating how each of the substantive standards (noise, lighting, waste heat, water use, and waste management) will be met in the construction and operation of the data center. e Fails to require monitoring during construction and operation to validate the planning and mitigation projections and to demonstrate compliance.
Lacking are specific standards for approval or denial of a data center CUP.

What do the revisions accomplish? e Underground space would no longer be usable for a data center. e Broadens setbacks to include nursing homes, hospitals, residential care facility, rehabilitation home, traditional housing, homeless shelter.

Increases setbacks from 100 to 200 feet for certain existing land uses, for 50,001 — 250,000 sq ft data centers. e Clarifies that generators are for emergency use only. e Requires street trees as part of landscaping along public ROWs. e Clarifies that a power plant or alternative energy system needs to be separately permitted. e Provides more detail on what the low-impact site design standards require when they say to “maximize” or “minimize,” but in so doing reduces the obligations to the specified minimum or maximum percentages of existing tree canopy, impervious surface, and land slope.

sentences: As Kentucky looks toward the future, the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure has led to surging demand for data centers and energy resources across our country.

Data center companies looking to do business in Kentucky, at a minimum, must demonstrate they will be good neighbors by investing responsibly, operating transparently, and working in partnership with our people and communities to make certain these projects deliver lasting benefits for Kentucky’s working families.

Data center project developers are required to submit an energy plan to the Energy and Environment Cabinet showing how it will protect residential ratepayers, including assurances it can meet its energy needs now, into the near term, and long term without imposing additional costs on other utility ratepayers.
The Public Service Commission shall not allow a utility to increase rates paid by other ratepayers to recover costs caused by the development and operation of a data center.

The Energy and Environment Cabinet is directed to deny any permitting applications where a data center would negatively impact Kentucky’s air quality, water use, water quality, water supply, federal jurisdictional wetlands, or natural resources.

Data center developers must also TH 局 의 ANDY BESHEAR GOVERNOR EXECUTIVE ORDER Secretary of State 2026-494 Frankfort August 6, 2026 Kentucky demonstrate compliance with all applicable environmental laws and public engagement requirements.
Data center project developers must commit to paying their full and fair share of state and local taxes and not attempt to avoid paying taxes, especially those for our local communities and schools.

Data center project developers must commit to engaging in public discussions with local community leaders and members where the project is proposing to locate, addressing with full transparency the community’s questions, including how the data center will create local job opportunities.
Nothing in this Order shall impact decisions made by local communities regarding the operation of data centers within their jurisdiction.
My Office will actively monitor data center projects and hold them accountable for the commitments they make to our local communities and people.

records.item: AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE LOUISVILLE METRO LAND DEVELOPMENT CODE REGARDING DATA CENTERS (CASE NO. 25-LDC-0014). O-251-26
sentences: Text Amendment to the Land Development Code for Data Centers APPLICANT:

Chapter 1, Part 2 Definitions **** Data Center – All or portion of a facility used primarily for data services, including the storage, processing, management, and distribution of data through the use of computer systems, servers, networking equipment, and related components.
Data Center, Accessory – A Data Center that serves a Principal Use on the same lot, while subordinate in purpose to other on-site activities of the Principal Use.

Although an Accessory Data Center’s primary purpose is to provide data infrastructure supporting the operation of an on-site Principal Use, it may support the enterprise functions of the business, institution, or organization associated with the on-site Principal Use.
Data Center, Telecommunication – A Data Center that exclusively serves a Telecommunication Facility and/or a telecommunications service provider or providers.

Data Center, White Space – The usable area within a Data Center specifically allocated for housing IT equipment, such as servers, storage arrays, and networking hardware. **** Chapter 2 Part 4 Commercial Zoning Districts **** 2.4.5 C-3 Commercial District **** A.

The following uses of underground space may be permitted upon the granting of a Conditional Use Permit: **** • Computer data center. **** 4.2.68 Data Centers (50,000 Square Feet or Less of Floor Area) Any Data Center that does not meet the provisions of Section 4.3.35 may be allowed in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, and PRO districts upon the granting of a conditional use permit and compliance with the listed requirements.
The Data Center shall be located in a Campus, Regional Center, Suburban Workplace, or Traditional Workplace Form District.

Any Conditional Use Permit is subject to the applicant also receiving all necessary permits from local, state and federal regulatory agencies. 4.2.69 Data Centers (50,001 to 500,000 Square Feet of Floor Area) Data Centers having greater than 50,000 square feet of floor area may be allowed in the M-1 district upon the granting of a conditional use permit and compliance with the listed requirements.

Any increase in the square footage of White Space at a lawfully nonconforming Data Center that was established prior to the effective date of the requirements in this section shall require a Conditional Use Permit for the development site and new development associated with the expansion shall be in compliance with this section.
The Data Center White Space and any other floor area that exclusively supports the Data Center shall not exceed 500,000 square feet in total floor area on the development site.
If otherwise permitted, additional floor area may be allowed for other non- Data Center uses on the development site (e.g. office).

COUNCIL MEMBERS CHAPPELL, PARRISH-WRIGHT, AND HAWKINS WHEREAS, the Legislative Council of the Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Government (the “Council”) passed Resolution No. 082, Series 2025 requesting the Planning Commission review the Land Development Code regarding Data Centers on September 25, 2025; and WHEREAS, the expectation was that the review would take approximately six (6) months to complete (by March 25, 2026), with the resolution requesting Planning Commission recommendations within one hundred twenty (120) days of passage (by January 23, 2026); and;

There is hereby imposed a moratorium on the acceptance and further processing by Louisville Metro Planning & Design Services, Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Planning Commission, and Louisville/Jefferson County Board of Zoning Adjustment of any applications for rezoning, conditional use permits, and Plan Certain, Category 2B and 3 development plans that propose telecommunications hotels and/or data centers as one or more of the proposed uses.

records.title: 25-LDC-0014_Data Center_ 09-03-26 DRAFT Amendments (Conceptually Approved by PC on 8-20-26).pdf
records.item: Request: Text Amendment to the Land Development Code Project Name: Data Centers Applicant: Louisville Metro Jurisdiction: Louisville Metro Council District: All Council Districts Case Manager: Joseph Haberman, AICP, Planning & Design Manager 25-LDC-0014...
sentences: Text Amendment to the Land Development Code for Data Centers APPLICANT:

Chapter 1, Part 2 Definitions **** Data Center – All or portion of a facility used primarily for data services, including the storage, processing, management, and distribution of data through the use of computer systems, servers, networking equipment, and related components.
Data Center, Accessory – A Data Center that serves a Principal Use on the same lot, while subordinate in purpose to other on-site activities of the Principal Use.

Although an Accessory Data Center’s primary purpose is to provide data infrastructure supporting the operation of an on-site Principal Use, it may support the enterprise functions of the business, institution, or organization associated with the on-site Principal Use.
Data Center, Telecommunication – A Data Center that exclusively serves a Telecommunication Facility and/or a telecommunications service provider or providers.

Data Center, White Space – The usable area within a Data Center specifically allocated for housing IT equipment, such as servers, storage arrays, and networking hardware. **** Chapter 2 Part 4 Commercial Zoning Districts **** 2.4.5 C-3 Commercial District **** A.

The following uses of underground space may be permitted upon the granting of a Conditional Use Permit: **** • Computer data center. **** 4.2.68 Data Centers (50,000 Square Feet or Less of Floor Area) Any Data Center that does not meet the provisions of Section 4.3.35 may be allowed in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, and PRO districts upon the granting of a conditional use permit and compliance with the listed requirements.
The Data Center shall be located in a Campus, Regional Center, Suburban Workplace, or Traditional Workplace Form District.

records.item: Request: Text Amendment to the Land Development Code Project Name: Data Centers Applicant: Louisville Metro Jurisdiction: Louisville Metro Council District: All Council Districts Case Manager: Joseph Haberman, AICP, Planning & Design Manager 25-LDC-0014..
sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.

sentences: Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org August 7, 2026 Joseph Haberman, AICP Planning & Design Manager Via email Re: 25 LDC 0014 Revised Text Amendment to Land Development Code For Data Centers Dear Mr.
(KRC) regarding the proposed revised Louisville Metro Government Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC- 0014, July 20, 2026, Draft).

Sincerely, Ashley Wilmes Executive Director and Attorney Kentucky Resources Council Tom FitzGerald Of Counsel Kentucky Resources Council Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org KRC Recommended Revisions to Louisville Metro Revised Draft Data Center Text Amendments This document presents the recommendations of Kentucky Resources Council concerning the revised Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC- 0014, July 20, 2026, Draft).

Introduction These recommendations are intended to ensure public notice and input, as well as a comprehensive and meaningful framework for regulating the location, operation, and decommissioning of all data centers.

The recommendations continue to suggest inclusion of many of the provisions in the Kentucky Resources Council (KRC) Model Data Center Zoning Ordinance, with respect to strengthening the review process, the quality of information submitted in applications, and the standards of performance for data center construction and operation.

Few of the recommendations on the initial draft were incorporated into the current draft, and it is hoped that with further reflection, more of these concerns will be addressed in order to assure that data center siting, location, operation, and decommissioning will be done, if at all, in order to fully mitigate impacts and to respect other land uses and values.

Recommendations The July 20, 2026 revisions to the proposed Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, (and in some areas weaken the protections in the original draft), so that the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
Eliminate tiered approach to data center regulation.

The LMG text amendment takes a size-tiered approach, prohibiting data centers exceeding 500,000 square feet, requiring a conditional use permit for facilities between 250,001 and 500,000 square feet and treating smaller facilities as permitted uses with special standards in various industrial districts, subject only to registration with the Office of Planning and review by the Planning Director or designee, with no public notice or hearing opportunity.
With few exceptions, the LMG text amendment proposes the same standards and requirements for all tiers of data centers.
Yet for data center proposals below 250,000 square feet, the review process is abridged and public notice and comment eliminated in almost all instances.

KRC believes that the same standards and review process, including robust public involvement, should apply to all data centers that are subject to regulation, since those standards are self-differentiating and self-adjusting depending on the size, nature and intensity of the use. 2.

records.item: Request: Text Amendment to the Land Development Code Project Name: Data Centers Applicant: Louisville Metro Jurisdiction: Louisville Metro Council District: All Council Districts Case Manager: Joseph Haberman, AICP, Planning & Design Manager 25-LDC-0014,
sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.

Data centers are buildings that house computer hardware that stores and processes digital information.
Currently, data centers are not classified as a specific use in the LDC.
Data centers that are in accessory in nature can be permitted in any zoning district in accordance with the accessory use standards.

In addition, “computer data centers” are listed as an acceptable activity for the underground space use, which is permitted with a conditional use permit in M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, PRO, C-M, C-2, and EZ-1.

Restrict data centers between 50,000 and 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the EZ-1, M-2, M- 3, and PEC districts and subject to special standards; and 4.

Only permit data centers that are less than 50,000 sq ft to manufacturing/ industrial areas in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC and PRO districts and subject to special standards (with an exception for telecommunication data centers in the C-3 district).

records.title: 25-LDC-0014_Kentucky Resources Council Recommended Ordinance_Version 1.4.pdf
records.item: Request: Text Amendment to the Land Development Code Project Name: Data Centers Applicant: Louisville Metro Jurisdiction: Louisville Metro Council District: All Council Districts Case Manager: Joseph Haberman, AICP, Planning & Design Manager 25-LDC-0014.
sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.

Data centers are buildings that house computer hardware that stores and processes digital information.
Currently, data centers are not classified as a specific use in the LDC.
Data centers that are in accessory in nature can be permitted in any zoning district in accordance with the accessory use standards.

Only permit data centers that are less than 50,000 sq ft to manufacturing/ industrial areas in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC and PRO districts and subject to special standards (with an exception for telecommunication data centers in the C-3 district).

records.item: Request: Text Amendment to the Land Development Code Project Name: Data Centers Applicant: Louisville Metro Jurisdiction: Louisville Metro Council District: All Council Districts Case Manager: Joseph Haberman, AICP, Planning & Design Manager 25-LDC-0014
sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.

sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.

sentences: Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org August 7, 2026 Joseph Haberman, AICP Planning & Design Manager Via email Re: 25 LDC 0014 Revised Text Amendment to Land Development Code For Data Centers Dear Mr.
(KRC) regarding the proposed revised Louisville Metro Government Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC- 0014, July 20, 2026, Draft).

Sincerely, Ashley Wilmes Executive Director and Attorney Kentucky Resources Council Tom FitzGerald Of Counsel Kentucky Resources Council Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org KRC Recommended Revisions to Louisville Metro Revised Draft Data Center Text Amendments This document presents the recommendations of Kentucky Resources Council concerning the revised Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC- 0014, July 20, 2026, Draft).

Introduction These recommendations are intended to ensure public notice and input, as well as a comprehensive and meaningful framework for regulating the location, operation, and decommissioning of all data centers.

The recommendations continue to suggest inclusion of many of the provisions in the Kentucky Resources Council (KRC) Model Data Center Zoning Ordinance, with respect to strengthening the review process, the quality of information submitted in applications, and the standards of performance for data center construction and operation.

Few of the recommendations on the initial draft were incorporated into the current draft, and it is hoped that with further reflection, more of these concerns will be addressed in order to assure that data center siting, location, operation, and decommissioning will be done, if at all, in order to fully mitigate impacts and to respect other land uses and values.

Recommendations The July 20, 2026 revisions to the proposed Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, (and in some areas weaken the protections in the original draft), so that the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
Eliminate tiered approach to data center regulation.

The LMG text amendment takes a size-tiered approach, prohibiting data centers exceeding 500,000 square feet, requiring a conditional use permit for facilities between 250,001 and 500,000 square feet and treating smaller facilities as permitted uses with special standards in various industrial districts, subject only to registration with the Office of Planning and review by the Planning Director or designee, with no public notice or hearing opportunity.
With few exceptions, the LMG text amendment proposes the same standards and requirements for all tiers of data centers.
Yet for data center proposals below 250,000 square feet, the review process is abridged and public notice and comment eliminated in almost all instances.

KRC believes that the same standards and review process, including robust public involvement, should apply to all data centers that are subject to regulation, since those standards are self-differentiating and self-adjusting depending on the size, nature and intensity of the use. 2.

Text Amendment to the Land Development Code (LDC) related to Data Centers • Staff finds the text amendment is in keeping with Plan 2040 and recommends that the Planning Commission RECOMMEND that the Louisville Metro Council and other legislative bodies with zoning authority APPROVE the text amendment presented in this report CASE SUMMARY The Louisville Metro Council passed a resolution on September 25, 2025 requesting that staff and the Planning Commission review the Land Development Code (LDC) and develop recommendations to improve the regulations for data centers.
Data centers are buildings that house computer hardware that stores and processes digital information.
Currently, data centers are not classified as a specific use in the LDC.
Data centers that are in accessory in nature can be permitted in any zoning district in accordance with the accessory use standards.

In addition, “computer data centers” are listed as an acceptable activity for the underground space use, which is permitted with a conditional use permit in M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, PRO, C-M, C-2, and EZ-1.

Prohibit future data centers exceeding 500,000 sq ft, while allowing smaller-scale facilities that support existing employers and business needs within the community to more appropriate areas based on their size;
Restrict data centers that are over 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the M-3 district with a conditional use permit; 3.
Restrict data centers between 50,000 and 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the EZ-1, M-2, M- 3, and PEC districts and subject to special standards; and 4.

Only permit data centers that are less than 50,000 sq ft to manufacturing/ industrial areas in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC and PRO districts and subject to special standards (with an exception for telecommunication data centers in the C-3 district).

sentences: Feedback on Revised Draft Regulations on Data Centers Dear Commissioners, Louisville Climate Action Network (LCAN) consists of 68 entities —36 non-profit groups, 17 forprofit businesses, 1] faith-based organizations and four educational institutions—plus well over 3,000 individuals, all concerned about climate change, public health and utility affordability.

Citizens all over the US are calling on local governments to protect them from the harms posed by hyper-scale data centers, especially huge demands for power and water—risking reliability and rate hikes for everyone—air pollution and noise.

OPO —— Council Dee 126 www.kyrc.org ol KRC Summary of Revisions to Louisville Data Center Ordinance This document reviews the changes in the provisions of the proposed Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC-0014, June 9, 2026, Draft, revised following comment period on July 20, 2026.

The text of the revised proposed regulations, public comment form, and schedule for the public hearing dates for the Planning Commission to hear public comment are at: lidips://iouisvillekv.wouv/euveruuenl /olive-piduiiuy/Gala-cenlers Summary The revisions proposed to the draft Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, and the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
The review process remains at Director level or below for data centers of up to 250,000 sq. ft. in size unless a waiver is needed.

Revised proposal instead weakens the initial LMG proposal by eliminating conditional use permit requirement for telecommunications data centers except for those 50,001 to 250,000 that can't meet special standards.

The applicant is not required to submit plans as part of the application, demonstrating how each of the substantive standards (noise, lighting, waste heat, water use, and waste management) will be met in the construction and operation of the data center. e Fails to require monitoring during construction and operation to validate the planning and mitigation projections and to demonstrate compliance.
Lacking are specific standards for approval or denial of a data center CUP.

What do the revisions accomplish? e Underground space would no longer be usable for a data center. e Broadens setbacks to include nursing homes, hospitals, residential care facility, rehabilitation home, traditional housing, homeless shelter.

Increases setbacks from 100 to 200 feet for certain existing land uses, for 50,001 — 250,000 sq ft data centers. e Clarifies that generators are for emergency use only. e Requires street trees as part of landscaping along public ROWs. e Clarifies that a power plant or alternative energy system needs to be separately permitted. e Provides more detail on what the low-impact site design standards require when they say to “maximize” or “minimize,” but in so doing reduces the obligations to the specified minimum or maximum percentages of existing tree canopy, impervious surface, and land slope.

records.item: AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE LOUISVILLE METRO LAND DEVELOPMENT CODE REGARDING DATA CENTERS (CASE NO. 25-LDC-0014). O-251-26
sentences: As Kentucky looks toward the future, the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure has led to surging demand for data centers and energy resources across our country.

Data center companies looking to do business in Kentucky, at a minimum, must demonstrate they will be good neighbors by investing responsibly, operating transparently, and working in partnership with our people and communities to make certain these projects deliver lasting benefits for Kentucky’s working families.

Data center project developers are required to submit an energy plan to the Energy and Environment Cabinet showing how it will protect residential ratepayers, including assurances it can meet its energy needs now, into the near term, and long term without imposing additional costs on other utility ratepayers.
The Public Service Commission shall not allow a utility to increase rates paid by other ratepayers to recover costs caused by the development and operation of a data center.

The Energy and Environment Cabinet is directed to deny any permitting applications where a data center would negatively impact Kentucky’s air quality, water use, water quality, water supply, federal jurisdictional wetlands, or natural resources.

Data center developers must also TH 局 의 ANDY BESHEAR GOVERNOR EXECUTIVE ORDER Secretary of State 2026-494 Frankfort August 6, 2026 Kentucky demonstrate compliance with all applicable environmental laws and public engagement requirements.
Data center project developers must commit to paying their full and fair share of state and local taxes and not attempt to avoid paying taxes, especially those for our local communities and schools.

Data center project developers must commit to engaging in public discussions with local community leaders and members where the project is proposing to locate, addressing with full transparency the community’s questions, including how the data center will create local job opportunities.
Nothing in this Order shall impact decisions made by local communities regarding the operation of data centers within their jurisdiction.
My Office will actively monitor data center projects and hold them accountable for the commitments they make to our local communities and people.

Chapter 1, Part 2 Definitions **** Data Center – All or portion of a facility used primarily for data services, including the storage, processing, management, and distribution of data through the use of computer systems, servers, networking equipment, and related components.

records.item: AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE LOUISVILLE METRO LAND DEVELOPMENT CODE REGARDING DATA CENTERS (CASE NO. 25-LDC-0014). O-251-26
sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.

sentences: Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org August 7, 2026 Joseph Haberman, AICP Planning & Design Manager Via email Re: 25 LDC 0014 Revised Text Amendment to Land Development Code For Data Centers Dear Mr.

Sincerely, Ashley Wilmes Executive Director and Attorney Kentucky Resources Council Tom FitzGerald Of Counsel Kentucky Resources Council Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org KRC Recommended Revisions to Louisville Metro Revised Draft Data Center Text Amendments This document presents the recommendations of Kentucky Resources Council concerning the revised Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC- 0014, July 20, 2026, Draft).

Introduction These recommendations are intended to ensure public notice and input, as well as a comprehensive and meaningful framework for regulating the location, operation, and decommissioning of all data centers.

The recommendations continue to suggest inclusion of many of the provisions in the Kentucky Resources Council (KRC) Model Data Center Zoning Ordinance, with respect to strengthening the review process, the quality of information submitted in applications, and the standards of performance for data center construction and operation.

Few of the recommendations on the initial draft were incorporated into the current draft, and it is hoped that with further reflection, more of these concerns will be addressed in order to assure that data center siting, location, operation, and decommissioning will be done, if at all, in order to fully mitigate impacts and to respect other land uses and values.

Recommendations The July 20, 2026 revisions to the proposed Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, (and in some areas weaken the protections in the original draft), so that the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
Eliminate tiered approach to data center regulation.

The LMG text amendment takes a size-tiered approach, prohibiting data centers exceeding 500,000 square feet, requiring a conditional use permit for facilities between 250,001 and 500,000 square feet and treating smaller facilities as permitted uses with special standards in various industrial districts, subject only to registration with the Office of Planning and review by the Planning Director or designee, with no public notice or hearing opportunity.
With few exceptions, the LMG text amendment proposes the same standards and requirements for all tiers of data centers.
Yet for data center proposals below 250,000 square feet, the review process is abridged and public notice and comment eliminated in almost all instances.

KRC believes that the same standards and review process, including robust public involvement, should apply to all data centers that are subject to regulation, since those standards are self-differentiating and self-adjusting depending on the size, nature and intensity of the use. 2.

Text Amendment to the Land Development Code (LDC) related to Data Centers • Staff finds the text amendment is in keeping with Plan 2040 and recommends that the Planning Commission RECOMMEND that the Louisville Metro Council and other legislative bodies with zoning authority APPROVE the text amendment presented in this report CASE SUMMARY The Louisville Metro Council passed a resolution on September 25, 2025 requesting that staff and the Planning Commission review the Land Development Code (LDC) and develop recommendations to improve the regulations for data centers.
Data centers are buildings that house computer hardware that stores and processes digital information.
Currently, data centers are not classified as a specific use in the LDC.
Data centers that are in accessory in nature can be permitted in any zoning district in accordance with the accessory use standards.

In addition, “computer data centers” are listed as an acceptable activity for the underground space use, which is permitted with a conditional use permit in M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, PRO, C-M, C-2, and EZ-1.

Prohibit future data centers exceeding 500,000 sq ft, while allowing smaller-scale facilities that support existing employers and business needs within the community to more appropriate areas based on their size;
Restrict data centers that are over 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the M-3 district with a conditional use permit; 3.
Restrict data centers between 50,000 and 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the EZ-1, M-2, M- 3, and PEC districts and subject to special standards; and 4.

Only permit data centers that are less than 50,000 sq ft to manufacturing/ industrial areas in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC and PRO districts and subject to special standards (with an exception for telecommunication data centers in the C-3 district).

TECHNICAL REVIEW As data centers are currently permitted by right and do not require any local license or registration, the number of existing data centers is not tracked by any Louisville Metro Government agency.
Datacentermap.com, an online resource that provides locations and information related to data centers, indicated that were 23 data centers in Louisville as of July 23, 2026.

OPO —— Council Dee 126 www.kyrc.org ol KRC Summary of Revisions to Louisville Data Center Ordinance This document reviews the changes in the provisions of the proposed Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC-0014, June 9, 2026, Draft, revised following comment period on July 20, 2026.

The text of the revised proposed regulations, public comment form, and schedule for the public hearing dates for the Planning Commission to hear public comment are at: lidips://iouisvillekv.wouv/euveruuenl /olive-piduiiuy/Gala-cenlers Summary The revisions proposed to the draft Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, and the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
The review process remains at Director level or below for data centers of up to 250,000 sq. ft. in size unless a waiver is needed.

Revised proposal instead weakens the initial LMG proposal by eliminating conditional use permit requirement for telecommunications data centers except for those 50,001 to 250,000 that can't meet special standards.

The applicant is not required to submit plans as part of the application, demonstrating how each of the substantive standards (noise, lighting, waste heat, water use, and waste management) will be met in the construction and operation of the data center. e Fails to require monitoring during construction and operation to validate the planning and mitigation projections and to demonstrate compliance.
Lacking are specific standards for approval or denial of a data center CUP.

What do the revisions accomplish? e Underground space would no longer be usable for a data center. e Broadens setbacks to include nursing homes, hospitals, residential care facility, rehabilitation home, traditional housing, homeless shelter.

Increases setbacks from 100 to 200 feet for certain existing land uses, for 50,001 — 250,000 sq ft data centers. e Clarifies that generators are for emergency use only. e Requires street trees as part of landscaping along public ROWs. e Clarifies that a power plant or alternative energy system needs to be separately permitted. e Provides more detail on what the low-impact site design standards require when they say to “maximize” or “minimize,” but in so doing reduces the obligations to the specified minimum or maximum percentages of existing tree canopy, impervious surface, and land slope.

sentences: As Kentucky looks toward the future, the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure has led to surging demand for data centers and energy resources across our country.

Data center companies looking to do business in Kentucky, at a minimum, must demonstrate they will be good neighbors by investing responsibly, operating transparently, and working in partnership with our people and communities to make certain these projects deliver lasting benefits for Kentucky’s working families.

Data center project developers are required to submit an energy plan to the Energy and Environment Cabinet showing how it will protect residential ratepayers, including assurances it can meet its energy needs now, into the near term, and long term without imposing additional costs on other utility ratepayers.
The Public Service Commission shall not allow a utility to increase rates paid by other ratepayers to recover costs caused by the development and operation of a data center.

The Energy and Environment Cabinet is directed to deny any permitting applications where a data center would negatively impact Kentucky’s air quality, water use, water quality, water supply, federal jurisdictional wetlands, or natural resources.

Data center developers must also TH 局 의 ANDY BESHEAR GOVERNOR EXECUTIVE ORDER Secretary of State 2026-494 Frankfort August 6, 2026 Kentucky demonstrate compliance with all applicable environmental laws and public engagement requirements.
Data center project developers must commit to paying their full and fair share of state and local taxes and not attempt to avoid paying taxes, especially those for our local communities and schools.

Data center project developers must commit to engaging in public discussions with local community leaders and members where the project is proposing to locate, addressing with full transparency the community’s questions, including how the data center will create local job opportunities.

sentences: 25-LDC-0014 Planning Commission Staff Report July 25, 2026 Text Amendment to the Land Development Code – Data Center Location:

Text Amendment to the Land Development Code (LDC) related to Data Centers • Staff finds the text amendment is in keeping with Plan 2040 and recommends that the Planning Commission RECOMMEND that the Louisville Metro Council and other legislative bodies with zoning authority APPROVE the text amendment presented in this report CASE SUMMARY The Louisville Metro Council passed a resolution on September 25, 2025 requesting that staff and the Planning Commission review the Land Development Code (LDC) and develop recommendations to improve the regulations for data centers.
Data centers are buildings that house computer hardware that stores and processes digital information.
Currently, data centers are not classified as a specific use in the LDC.
Data centers that are in accessory in nature can be permitted in any zoning district in accordance with the accessory use standards.

In addition, “computer data centers” are listed as an acceptable activity for the underground space use, which is permitted with a conditional use permit in M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, PRO, C-M, C-2, and EZ-1.

Prohibit future data centers exceeding 500,000 sq ft, while allowing smaller-scale facilities that support existing employers and business needs within the community to more appropriate areas based on their size;
Restrict data centers that are over 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the M-3 district with a conditional use permit; 3.
Restrict data centers between 50,000 and 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the EZ-1, M-2, M- 3, and PEC districts and subject to special standards; and 4.

Only permit data centers that are less than 50,000 sq ft to manufacturing/ industrial areas in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC and PRO districts and subject to special standards (with an exception for telecommunication data centers in the C-3 district).

TECHNICAL REVIEW As data centers are currently permitted by right and do not require any local license or registration, the number of existing data centers is not tracked by any Louisville Metro Government agency.
Datacentermap.com, an online resource that provides locations and information related to data centers, indicated that were 23 data centers in Louisville as of July 23, 2026.

sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.

sentences: Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org August 7, 2026 Joseph Haberman, AICP Planning & Design Manager Via email Re: 25 LDC 0014 Revised Text Amendment to Land Development Code For Data Centers Dear Mr.
(KRC) regarding the proposed revised Louisville Metro Government Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC- 0014, July 20, 2026, Draft).

Sincerely, Ashley Wilmes Executive Director and Attorney Kentucky Resources Council Tom FitzGerald Of Counsel Kentucky Resources Council Post Office Box 1070 Frankfort, Kentucky 40602 502-875-2428 hello@kyrc.org www.kyrc.org KRC Recommended Revisions to Louisville Metro Revised Draft Data Center Text Amendments This document presents the recommendations of Kentucky Resources Council concerning the revised Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC- 0014, July 20, 2026, Draft).

Introduction These recommendations are intended to ensure public notice and input, as well as a comprehensive and meaningful framework for regulating the location, operation, and decommissioning of all data centers.

The recommendations continue to suggest inclusion of many of the provisions in the Kentucky Resources Council (KRC) Model Data Center Zoning Ordinance, with respect to strengthening the review process, the quality of information submitted in applications, and the standards of performance for data center construction and operation.

Few of the recommendations on the initial draft were incorporated into the current draft, and it is hoped that with further reflection, more of these concerns will be addressed in order to assure that data center siting, location, operation, and decommissioning will be done, if at all, in order to fully mitigate impacts and to respect other land uses and values.

Recommendations The July 20, 2026 revisions to the proposed Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, (and in some areas weaken the protections in the original draft), so that the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
Eliminate tiered approach to data center regulation.

The LMG text amendment takes a size-tiered approach, prohibiting data centers exceeding 500,000 square feet, requiring a conditional use permit for facilities between 250,001 and 500,000 square feet and treating smaller facilities as permitted uses with special standards in various industrial districts, subject only to registration with the Office of Planning and review by the Planning Director or designee, with no public notice or hearing opportunity.
With few exceptions, the LMG text amendment proposes the same standards and requirements for all tiers of data centers.
Yet for data center proposals below 250,000 square feet, the review process is abridged and public notice and comment eliminated in almost all instances.

KRC believes that the same standards and review process, including robust public involvement, should apply to all data centers that are subject to regulation, since those standards are self-differentiating and self-adjusting depending on the size, nature and intensity of the use. 2.

Text Amendment to the Land Development Code (LDC) related to Data Centers • Staff finds the text amendment is in keeping with Plan 2040 and recommends that the Planning Commission RECOMMEND that the Louisville Metro Council and other legislative bodies with zoning authority APPROVE the text amendment presented in this report CASE SUMMARY The Louisville Metro Council passed a resolution on September 25, 2025 requesting that staff and the Planning Commission review the Land Development Code (LDC) and develop recommendations to improve the regulations for data centers.
Data centers are buildings that house computer hardware that stores and processes digital information.
Currently, data centers are not classified as a specific use in the LDC.
Data centers that are in accessory in nature can be permitted in any zoning district in accordance with the accessory use standards.

In addition, “computer data centers” are listed as an acceptable activity for the underground space use, which is permitted with a conditional use permit in M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC, PRO, C-M, C-2, and EZ-1.

Prohibit future data centers exceeding 500,000 sq ft, while allowing smaller-scale facilities that support existing employers and business needs within the community to more appropriate areas based on their size;
Restrict data centers that are over 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the M-3 district with a conditional use permit; 3.
Restrict data centers between 50,000 and 250,000 sq ft to industrial areas in the EZ-1, M-2, M- 3, and PEC districts and subject to special standards; and 4.

Only permit data centers that are less than 50,000 sq ft to manufacturing/ industrial areas in the C-M, EZ-1, M-1, M-2, M-3, PEC and PRO districts and subject to special standards (with an exception for telecommunication data centers in the C-3 district).

sentences: Feedback on Revised Draft Regulations on Data Centers Dear Commissioners, Louisville Climate Action Network (LCAN) consists of 68 entities —36 non-profit groups, 17 forprofit businesses, 1] faith-based organizations and four educational institutions—plus well over 3,000 individuals, all concerned about climate change, public health and utility affordability.

Citizens all over the US are calling on local governments to protect them from the harms posed by hyper-scale data centers, especially huge demands for power and water—risking reliability and rate hikes for everyone—air pollution and noise.
Data center power demands and diesel-powered backup generators alone demand that LCAN respond to the latest revised draft ordinance changes now before you on behalf of our members.
As written, the much touted “ban” on data centers larger than 500,00 ft? is flawed, since the ordinance doesn’t preclude two, side-by-side 499,000 ft? data centers on adjacent tracts.

OPO —— Council Dee 126 www.kyrc.org ol KRC Summary of Revisions to Louisville Data Center Ordinance This document reviews the changes in the provisions of the proposed Louisville Metro Government (“LMG”) Draft Data Center Land Development Code Text Amendment (Case No. 25-LDC-0014, June 9, 2026, Draft, revised following comment period on July 20, 2026.

The text of the revised proposed regulations, public comment form, and schedule for the public hearing dates for the Planning Commission to hear public comment are at: lidips://iouisvillekv.wouv/euveruuenl /olive-piduiiuy/Gala-cenlers Summary The revisions proposed to the draft Louisville Metro data center ordinance do not materially improve on the original draft, and the recommendations of KRC for a fundamental revision of the proposed code revisions remain largely unchanged.
The review process remains at Director level or below for data centers of up to 250,000 sq. ft. in size unless a waiver is needed.

Revised proposal instead weakens the initial LMG proposal by eliminating conditional use permit requirement for telecommunications data centers except for those 50,001 to 250,000 that can't meet special standards.

The applicant is not required to submit plans as part of the application, demonstrating how each of the substantive standards (noise, lighting, waste heat, water use, and waste management) will be met in the construction and operation of the data center. e Fails to require monitoring during construction and operation to validate the planning and mitigation projections and to demonstrate compliance.
Lacking are specific standards for approval or denial of a data center CUP.

What do the revisions accomplish? e Underground space would no longer be usable for a data center. e Broadens setbacks to include nursing homes, hospitals, residential care facility, rehabilitation home, traditional housing, homeless shelter.

Increases setbacks from 100 to 200 feet for certain existing land uses, for 50,001 — 250,000 sq ft data centers. e Clarifies that generators are for emergency use only. e Requires street trees as part of landscaping along public ROWs. e Clarifies that a power plant or alternative energy system needs to be separately permitted. e Provides more detail on what the low-impact site design standards require when they say to “maximize” or “minimize,” but in so doing reduces the obligations to the specified minimum or maximum percentages of existing tree canopy, impervious surface, and land slope.

records.item: AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE LOUISVILLE METRO LAND DEVELOPMENT CODE REGARDING DATA CENTERS (CASE NO. 25-LDC-0014). O-251-26
sentences: As Kentucky looks toward the future, the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure has led to surging demand for data centers and energy resources across our country.

Data center companies looking to do business in Kentucky, at a minimum, must demonstrate they will be good neighbors by investing responsibly, operating transparently, and working in partnership with our people and communities to make certain these projects deliver lasting benefits for Kentucky’s working families.

Data center project developers are required to submit an energy plan to the Energy and Environment Cabinet showing how it will protect residential ratepayers, including assurances it can meet its energy needs now, into the near term, and long term without imposing additional costs on other utility ratepayers.
The Public Service Commission shall not allow a utility to increase rates paid by other ratepayers to recover costs caused by the development and operation of a data center.

The Energy and Environment Cabinet is directed to deny any permitting applications where a data center would negatively impact Kentucky’s air quality, water use, water quality, water supply, federal jurisdictional wetlands, or natural resources.

Data center developers must also TH 局 의 ANDY BESHEAR GOVERNOR EXECUTIVE ORDER Secretary of State 2026-494 Frankfort August 6, 2026 Kentucky demonstrate compliance with all applicable environmental laws and public engagement requirements.
Data center project developers must commit to paying their full and fair share of state and local taxes and not attempt to avoid paying taxes, especially those for our local communities and schools.

Data center project developers must commit to engaging in public discussions with local community leaders and members where the project is proposing to locate, addressing with full transparency the community’s questions, including how the data center will create local job opportunities.
Nothing in this Order shall impact decisions made by local communities regarding the operation of data centers within their jurisdiction.
My Office will actively monitor data center projects and hold them accountable for the commitments they make to our local communities and people.

sentences: Data centers and data center development have recently become a concern across the country, as the development of new “artificial intelligence” tools has multiplied the demand for computer processing power, and correlative energy, water, and other resource needs.
At its base, a data center is a warehouse filled with racks of computer servers, often running all hours of the day and night.
As the size of data centers have grown, so has the need for ancillary equipment and resources both on- and off-site.
On-site, a data center also 1 This ordinance was developed for consideration and use by communities in the Commonwealth by the Kentucky Resources Council, Inc.
In addition, they also contain significant on-site backup or "behind-the-meter” power generating equipment, such as diesel generators, gas turbines, and battery energy storage systems.
To place the energy use of a typical data center in context, a currently proposed data center in Louisville, Kentucky is planned at 525 MW.
For an 85% capacity factor (proposed monthly average to qualify for a data center tariff), it would consume 3.90 TWh/year.

This is only slightly less than LG&E's 2023 total residential sales of 3.92 TWh, and would be more than 1/4 of the LG&E total (across all classes) winter coincident peak of 2,011 MW in 2022/23, or 20% of their summer peak of 2,639.
This means potentially that much backup generation capacity on-site, as well.

Common concerns of communities around data centers include: • Noise, both from computer cooling systems and backup generation; • Localized pollution, both from releases of contaminated cooling water to the air as vapor or to local waterways; • Energy and water consumption, and indirect impacts of that consumption on other utility customers’ bills.

The CUP process that KRC has proposed tracks closely with the site assessment review required of merchant electric generating plants under Kentucky’s Electric Generation and Transmission Siting Board.

This is intentional, since: • Data centers are often conceived and designed to co-locate with generation sources that are either not grid-tied or which are not utility-owned or operated, and which propose to generate electricity for the data center operations.
